# Selection — TRD §15 row 6: the anti-replay rule and envelope retention depth

**Status:** selected, and folded into the TRD. **Date:** 2026-08-19
**Closes:** TRD §15 row 6 · **Scope of:** review 3b (protocol)
**Constrained by:** TRD §7.4, §7.5, §7.6, §6.1, §14.3, §11.3 · **Stage:** [sequencing.md](../sequencing.md) §3.5
**Vectors:** [`test/vectors/antireplay.json`](../../test/vectors/antireplay.json), generated by
[`scripts/generate-antireplay-vectors.mjs`](../../scripts/generate-antireplay-vectors.mjs)
**Companions:** [row 4](./row-4-envelope-format.md) made `seq` one number and this row pays for it;
[row 5](./row-5-finalization.md) supplies the chain; [row 7](./row-7-checkpoint.md) supplies the baseline and
hands this row its interlock; [row 3](./row-3-record-format.md) supplies the carrier without changing.

---

## The selection

```
Admit an envelope at (credential c, position n)              four conditions

  1  It verifies                                              row 4
  2  n == held(c).seq + 1
  3  link_n is computed from the link the client itself holds  row 5
  4  a signed head at n verifies against THAT link, never
     the one the head carries                                  §7.5

  Otherwise HOLD — the position or its head has not arrived — or REFUSE.

  There is no fifth condition. "No second link at a position already
  held" needs no state: a second envelope at n arrives when the mark is
  already at n or beyond, and condition 2 refuses it.

Mint outbound                                                 row 4's cost

  Mint at own_held + 1. On a DEFINITE REFUSAL at n, re-mint at n.
  On no answer, WAIT — never re-mint. Re-minting a position that may
  have been accepted is self-equivocation, and condition 2 refuses it
  on every other device, permanently.

The local head vector                                         the carrier

  One (seq, link) per credential. A row 3 record with kind = 'heads',
  in its own object store, under the same store subkey, sharing the
  content store's `seq` sequence.

    plaintext = LP("done/heads/v1") || head_vector      row 7's, verbatim
    AAD       = row 3's record AAD, kind = 'heads'

  Write order: the content batch commits FIRST, the heads record after.

Retention                                                     three depths

  Own outbound envelopes  device | back to the SECOND-NEWEST admitted
                                 | checkpoint seen, not the newest
  Suffix beside a         store  | from that checkpoint's head vector
  checkpoint                     | forward, for each retained checkpoint
  Local head vector       device | a high-water mark, not a log

                LP(s) = uint16be(byteLength(utf8 s)) || utf8 s
```

Everything below is why, and what it cost.

---

## 1. The theorem the whole row rests on

A chain replayed from genesis and the same chain replayed from a checkpoint's head vector reach **the same
link at the same position**. The first vector is that equality, taken over twelve positions with a checkpoint
at nine.

It sounds like bookkeeping and it is the entire justification for every retention number below. Row 5's
guarantee is stated relative to a chain the client replayed itself; the obvious reading of that is _from
genesis_, and a client that believed it would retain every envelope forever. The equality says the chain has
no memory beyond its last link, so **a checkpoint's head vector is a chain state and not a summary of one** —
and everything below it can be dropped without weakening condition 3 at all.

Which means replaying from a checkpoint is not a special case with its own code path. It is the same loop with
a different starting value, and the generator runs it both ways round to say so.

---

## 2. The fifth condition, and why deleting it is the result

§7.5's _must not happen_ list ends with **no second link accepted at a position already held, however well
signed**. Written as a client rule that reads as a fifth condition needing its own state: a record of every
link ever admitted at every position, so a later arrival can be compared against it.

**It is implied by the second condition over a monotonic mark.** A second envelope at position 7 can only
arrive when the mark is at 7 or beyond, and condition 2 admits nothing that is not exactly one past the mark.
There is no moment at which a client holding a mark needs to consult a history to refuse.

That is not a simplification of the rule; it is the reason the carrier is one `(seq, link)` per credential
rather than a log that grows with every accepted write. **The rule as stated sounds like it needs the log, and
what actually needs it is nothing.** Two negatives publish both halves: the equivocated position offered below
the mark, refused by arithmetic, and the same one offered _at_ the mark, where the position check passes and
the signed head is what refuses it.

---

## 3. The re-mint hazard, which is this row's sharp edge

**Amended by [`S0-4`](../review/remediation/S0-4/README.md) (2026-08-27): the refusal this section requires had
no carrier.** It pointed at row 15's transition `Outcome`, which names a `(kind, workspace, lineage, target)` —
a transition, not an envelope — so it cannot say which credential, which position, or which exact digest was
never accepted (`f-745e332-envelope-refusal-carrier-missing`). TRD §7.5's `Refuse` is that object, signed by
`K_accept`, **permanent** over `(credential, position, digest, epoch)` — the epoch being the one the refused
envelope itself references, the fifth subject field the `S0-4` return added (`FU-06`): the client verifies
under the `K_accept` its lineage currently certifies, never a key taken from the answer, so a stale key's
genuine refusal is silence whichever epoch it names. The refusal licenses a successor that binds its
`refusal_id` — **at that refusal's own position and no other**, or skipping arrives through the back door. A
successor may itself be refused, and nothing caps the chain, or a credential stalls the second time an epoch
moves under it.

**`RC-4A` also proposed capping the *attempts* at one per refusal, and `S0-4` dropped it.** Every attempt at a
position competes for the one digest that position will ever accept, so this row's own rule already permits only
one of them to win. Removing the cap from the executable model changed no result — which is what *not
load-bearing* looks like when it is measured rather than argued.

**And _wait_ now has something to wait with.** This row said _never re-mint_ and left the client holding a
delta it cannot re-envelope identically; row 4's spool is where the exact bytes are, so silence means
**resubmit them**, which is safe whether the request was lost before arrival or the reply after acceptance.

[Row 4](./row-4-envelope-format.md) made `seq` the credential's outbound position and its accepted position as
one number, and recorded the cost: _a refused envelope stalls that credential's chain until it is re-minted at
the same position._ Read as a cost that is a delay. It is also a trap.

**The obvious recovery from a stall is the thing that breaks the chain permanently.** A client that has minted
position 7, waited, heard nothing and re-mints position 7 over whatever it has now — a perfectly reasonable
retry — produces a second, different link at a position the service may already have accepted. Every other
device refuses it under condition 2, permanently, and refusal there is _evidence of a compromised credential_.
An honest client has framed itself.

So the outbound rule has to distinguish two states that look identical from the client's side:

| What the client sees      | What it means                          | What it does                                              |
| ------------------------- | -------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| A definite refusal at _n_ | The service never accepted _n_         | Re-mint at _n_. Row 4 forbids skipping                    |
| No answer at _n_          | Unknown — accepted, in flight, or lost | **Wait**, and resubmit the identical bytes. Never re-mint |

A timeout is the second row, not the first. That distinction is invisible until it happens and retroactive
when it does, which is the same shape as row 2's nonce-reuse argument and deserves the same treatment: it is a
**must not happen** in §7.4 rather than a note in an implementation.

The vector for `equivocated-position-at-the-mark` is this case as well as the attacker's, and the file says so.
Nothing distinguishes an honest retry from a compromised credential, because there is nothing to distinguish
them by.

---

## 4. The carrier, and what row 3 already paid for

A device must persist its head vector because **it cannot recompute it.** Row 5's links are functions of
envelope digests; §7.4 retains a device's _own_ outbound envelopes only, and an inbound envelope is opened,
applied and gone. After a restart there is no other copy of `link` anywhere on the device.

**The mark carries a link and not just a number, and one negative is the whole argument.** §7.5 says a numeric
high-water mark is not a finalization boundary. One level down, a numeric mark is not an anti-replay state
either: a client that advanced a counter without keeping what it replayed cannot tell a chain it walked from
one it did not, and `numeric-mark-without-its-link` is that client being refused by the head it cannot match.

**The record is row 3's, with a third `kind`, and no format changed.** Row 3 bound `kind` in the AAD for a
stated attack — IndexedDB holds a structured clone whose properties the load path trusts, a `state` record
supersedes everything before it, and an editable `kind` is a way to make the store delete its own history
through its own trim path. That binding is what lets a third kind arrive here at no cost, and what stops a
heads record being reinterpreted as a `state` record and swept away. `heads-record-read-as-state` is row 3's
attack with a second victim.

So: **no sixth subkey, no new format, no new label except the one naming a plaintext body.** [Row
8](./row-8-attribution-record.md) declined a sixth subkey by finding where its records already belonged; this
is the same move at a smaller object, and it is available for the same reason.

**Two details that are not incidental.**

- **Its own object store**, so the content load path never sees a record it cannot apply as a Yjs update. The
  AAD's `kind` is what makes sharing the subkey across two stores safe rather than merely economical.
- **It shares the content store's `seq` sequence** rather than starting one. Row 3 argued its 12-byte random
  nonce budget from `seq` bounding the count of records under one generation _in one comparison_. Two
  sequences would make that two comparisons and a sum, so row 3's sentence **`seq` does not reset at trim**
  now also has to mean **`seq` is not per object store**. That is a word row 3 did not have to write because
  there was one store, and it is folded into §6.1.

---

## 5. The write order, and the direction that loses nothing

The content batch commits first; the heads record is written after it.

Reversed, a crash between the two leaves a mark at position 12 over content that stops at 11 — and position 11
is then **below the baseline forever**, so it can never be re-admitted and the operation is gone. In the
selected order the same crash leaves a mark at 10 over content that reaches 12: positions 11 and 12 are
re-delivered, re-verified, and produce identical links. Duplicate coverage, which is harmless.

This is §6.1's trim rule in a second place — _write the state record, wait for its transaction, only then
delete what it supersedes_ — and it is the same asymmetry: one order leaves redundancy and the other leaves a
hole. Worth stating rather than deriving twice.

---

## 6. Three retention depths, and §7.4 states one of them too shallowly

They look like one rule and they are three, serving different tests.

| What                       | Held by | Floor                                                 | Because                                 |
| -------------------------- | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Its own outbound envelopes | device  | the **second-newest** admitted checkpoint it has seen | §11.3 test 8, §14.3                     |
| Each checkpoint's suffix   | store   | that checkpoint's head vector forward                 | first sync from any retained checkpoint |
| The local head vector      | device  | none — a mark, not a log                              | anti-replay                             |

**§7.4 says a device retains its own outbound envelopes "at least back to the last checkpoint it has seen
admitted", and taken at face value that is one checkpoint too shallow.** Row 7 retains **two**, because §11.3
test 8 requires falling back to the next-newest when the newest is unavailable. §14.3 has each device
re-envelop its own suffix from the checkpoint it applied. Compose them and the case is ordinary: the newest
checkpoint is unavailable, every device applies the next-newest, and a device trimmed to the newest cannot
supply the suffix from the one it just applied. The "at least" makes the sentence not _wrong_, and an
implementer reading it for a number takes the number it names.

**The correction needs no protocol field, which is what makes it worth taking.** A device does not have to be
told the store's retention policy: it counts locally and drops below the second-newest checkpoint it has seen
admitted. That is exactly row 7's _at least two_ observed from the other end, and it degrades safely — a store
retaining more than two leaves the device conservative, never short.

**This is a restore-time failure, not a review-time one.** Everything passes until the day the newest
checkpoint is the one that is gone, which is the only day test 8 describes.

---

## 7. What a gap costs, and what retires it

Condition 2 means a missing position stalls that credential's chain. The bound on how long is worth writing
down, because _hold_ is a state a user can sit in.

- **A gap above the newest checkpoint is transient.** The envelope is in flight, or withheld — §7.5 already
  calls withholding availability rather than integrity, and permits it.
- **A gap below it cannot happen while retention held**, since the store retains each retained checkpoint's
  suffix and the checkpoint's own head vector is the baseline.
- **So a persistent gap is a durable-store failure**, and it presents as sync not being current rather than as
  silence. The client holds, and says so.

**A checkpoint retires a gap, and that gives cadence a second job row 7 did not name.** A checkpoint's head
vector is a chain state above the gap, and a device adopting it never asks about anything below. Row 7
grounded cadence in first-sync cost alone; it also bounds how long a lost envelope can stall a credential.
That is not a number this row can set either — there is still no service to measure — but it is a second input
to the same tunable, and §7.6 now says so.

**A checkpoint cannot manufacture coverage.** Its producer must have applied the operations to have snapshotted
them, so a producer missing position 11 publishes a head vector that stops at 10. The gap retires when some
device gets 11 and checkpoints past it, and not before.

---

## 8. The residual: local rollback, which the seal does not close

An attacker with profile write access can replace the heads record with **an earlier one they did not forge** —
a genuine record, validly sealed under the same subkey and the same AAD shape, from before the mark advanced.
An AAD authenticates a record. It cannot order two valid ones.

**The vectors publish this as a demonstration rather than as a negative, because it succeeds**, and an entry in
a `must_fail` list that does not fail is the exact defect the coverage audit exists to catch, one level up.

The bound, stated rather than left to be discovered:

1. **Rolling the mark back re-opens positions the client already applied.** Re-admitting them is idempotent in
   Yjs and produces identical links, so by itself the rollback does nothing.
2. **To exploit it an attacker needs a second link accepted at a re-opened position** — which needs a signed
   head over it, which needs the service to sign a second link at a position it has already closed.
3. **So the local rollback is exploitable only in collusion with the service** — and against a colluding
   service the guarantee is already exactly §7.5's stated bound: non-equivocating per credential and within one
   client's view, with a transparency log or gossip named as what would close it and declined.

This adds no new residual. It routes into one that is already written down, which is the useful outcome — and
it is worth noticing that §6.1's _an attacker who can write your journal can write your JavaScript_ does **not**
dispose of it. The profile-copy attacker of §13.3 never runs the origin's code.

---

## 9. What it costs

| Cost                     | Size                                                                              |
| ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Per admitted run, client | One SHA-256 per position, one Ed25519 verify per run                              |
| Persistent state         | One `(seq, link)` per credential — about 70 bytes each, replaced in place         |
| Writes                   | One record per inbound batch, on the asynchronous path                            |
| Retained by a device     | Its own outbound envelopes to the second-newest checkpoint rather than the newest |
| New keys                 | **None.** Row 3's store subkey                                                    |
| New formats              | **None.** Row 3's record, row 7's serialization                                   |
| Bundle                   | **Nothing.** SHA-256, AES-GCM and Ed25519 are WebCrypto (row 1)                   |

---

## 10. What Stage 1 owes, and what Stage 4 owes

**Stage 1 owes an empty object store.** The heads store belongs to a workspace with a lineage, which is Stage
4 — but IndexedDB creates object stores only inside a version-change transaction, so adding it later is a
version bump over a real deployment's data. Creating it empty at genesis costs one line and nothing else.
This is [row 13](./row-13-device-lock.md)'s custody record again, at a different object and for the same
reason: [sequencing.md](../sequencing.md) §2.1's class of migration is one that is free now and is not free
after the cutover.

**The trim must know the third kind**, and §11.1's no-plaintext-at-rest test should inspect the new store like
any other. Both are Stage 1 notes rather than Stage 4's, because the store exists from genesis.

**Not in this row.** How often a checkpoint is produced is [row 7](./row-7-checkpoint.md)'s, now with a second
input. What the durable store does when two devices checkpoint concurrently is Stage 4's. What a package
carries and how deep its suffix part reaches is [row 10](./row-10-portable-package.md)'s, which takes its depth
from §6 here.

---

## 11. The vectors

`node scripts/generate-antireplay-vectors.mjs` writes them; `--check` fails if they are stale, and
`pnpm check` now runs it with the other twelve.

**One scenario, thirteen negatives and three demonstrations.** The phone's twelve accepted positions through a
rotation between 9 and 10, checkpointed at 9 — placed there because row 7 forces a checkpoint under the new
generation before the old one may be dropped, so the checkpoint a device adopts is very often that one.

**Seven of the negatives are the heads record's AAD**, one field at a time, which is row 3's list at a third
`kind`. **Five are the rule**, and each isolates one condition:

- `position-does-not-follow` — condition 2, before any hashing.
- `numeric-mark-without-its-link` — the mark's number right and its link wrong. The argument for the carrier's
  shape.
- `equivocated-position-below-the-mark` — refused by arithmetic, which is why there is no fifth condition.
- `equivocated-position-at-the-mark` — refused by the head, and signed at position 7 on purpose so it does not
  also fail for being at the wrong position. A negative that fails for two reasons tests neither.
- `baseline-from-another-checkpoint` — a substituted baseline cannot be walked forward into agreement.

**Seventeen more are the refusal's** (`S0-4`, grown at the return): the nine bound fields one at a time, each
with the client's own envelope following the patch so the signature is the only thing left to refuse it;
**five genuine signatures for the wrong subject** — position, digest, credential, workspace and epoch, the
last two added at the return — where the service really signed the message and it is not about this envelope;
and three authority cases: an unsigned error body, a key no epoch certifies, and **a key certified only at a
retired epoch** (`FU-06`'s delayed old-key compromise), refused because the verifier resolves from the
lineage's current certification rather than from the answer.

**The three demonstrations all succeed, which is the point of each of them.** `self_equivocation` publishes the
two links at position 7 so _a different link at a held position_ is a value rather than a description.
`head_checked_against_its_carried_link` shows §7.5's _must not happen_ **working** — the defective check admits
a link the client never replayed, because verifying a head against the link it carries is satisfied by the head
being well-formed. `local_rollback` is §8's residual, opening.

**One thing this file deliberately does not re-test.** Row 5's link and head constructions are reused verbatim
and are audited in `finalization.json`; registering them again would duplicate that coverage and make a failure
here point at the wrong document.
